solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Speed of sportsmen running on pitch, initially

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece placed on another follows it, so the pitch letter comes first
initially asks for the opening letter of the word pitch
running suggests the sportsmen are moving about, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sports report praising how quickly players got moving on the field at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running' looks like a description of the players, but it signals the anagram; 'on' in an across clue puts the rearranged letters after the pitch's opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Promptness is quickness in acting, a synonym of speed in the sense of swiftness of response.

clue.text: Publicity material has right look, it's said

indicators.note: it's said tells the solver that the phrase is spoken, giving a sound-alike

parts.note: right means proper, and a gander is a look in British slang ('have a gander')

explanation.surface: An advert or flyer that looks correct, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: PROPER GANDER, said out loud, sounds like the answer. 'Have a gander' is British slang for 'take a look'.
explanation.definitionFit: Propaganda is material spread to promote a cause or viewpoint, a kind of publicity.

clue.text: Old theologian, peculiar

parts.note: DD, Doctor of Divinity, is a theologian's degree

explanation.surface: A description of an elderly, eccentric scholar of religion.
explanation.definitionFit: Odd and peculiar are synonyms, both meaning strange or unusual.

clue.text: Sherpas translated groups of words

indicators.note: translated suggests the word Sherpas is turned into something else, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Himalayan guides having their speech put into another language.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase is a small group of words forming a unit, so plural phrases are groups of words.

clue.text: Delicious drink out of new crate, fizzy

indicators.note: fizzy suggests bubbling agitation, so the letters of crate are shaken up

explanation.surface: A tasty, sparkling drink taken straight from a freshly opened crate.
explanation.definitionFit: Nectar is the drink of the gods in myth, and by extension any delicious beverage.

clue.text: One-way ticket left out for char

indicators.note: out signals that the letter for left is removed from the ticket word

parts.note: in Britain a one-way ticket is called a single

explanation.surface: Someone buying a one-way ticket and leaving it out for a cleaning lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'char' looks like a charwoman (a British cleaner), but it is the verb meaning to scorch.
explanation.definitionFit: To singe is to burn slightly on the surface, the same as to char or scorch.

clue.text: Percussion instrument — have a dispute about right one

indicators.note: about means around, so the dispute word goes around the other letters

parts.note: to tangle with someone is to have a dispute or fight with them
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Musicians arguing over which percussion instrument is the correct one.
explanation.definitionFit: A triangle is a steel rod bent into three sides and struck to sound, an orchestral percussion instrument.

clue.text: Command from frontier leader of battalion ignored

indicators.note: ignored means that letter is left out of the frontier word

parts.note: a frontier is a border between countries

indicators.note: leader of asks for the opening letter of battalion

explanation.surface: A military instruction sent from the border while the battalion's commander is disregarded.
explanation.definitionFit: An order is an instruction that must be obeyed, a synonym of command.

clue.text: False report in article penned by witty person

indicators.note: penned by means enclosed by, so the article goes inside the witty person

parts.note: a card is an amusing, witty or eccentric person
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A misleading newspaper piece written by a humorous columnist.
explanation.definitionFit: A canard is an unfounded rumour or false story deliberately spread.

clue.text: Sheer physical strength of beast might

parts.note: a brute is a beast or savage animal
might in the sense of power means force

explanation.surface: Describing the raw power of a mighty animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means strength used without skill or subtlety, mere physical power.

clue.text: Luminous discharge solar cell can show

indicators.note: can show means the words solar cell display the letters within them

explanation.surface: A solar cell producing a glowing electrical spark.
explanation.definitionFit: An electric arc is a glowing discharge of current across a gap, a luminous discharge.

clue.text: Dish cut into pieces the old American served up

parts.note: to chop is to cut into pieces

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: ye is an old form of the
US is short for American, as in the United States

explanation.surface: A recipe: food chopped into pieces and served by an old American cook.
explanation.definitionFit: Chop suey is a Chinese-American stir-fried dish of meat and vegetables.

clue.text: Musical — say Hair with different opening

parts.note: to say is to state

indicators.note: with different opening means the first letter of the word Hair is swapped for another

explanation.surface: A suggestion to retitle the musical Hair with a new opening number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hair' really is a musical, tempting a solver to treat it as the definition. Its first letter H is changed to F.
explanation.definitionFit: State Fair is a Rodgers and Hammerstein musical, adapted for stage from their film.

clue.text: Wake in a river, the one passing through York

parts.note: the River Ouse flows through the city of York in northern England

explanation.surface: A disturbance on the water behind a boat on York's river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wake' looks like a boat's trail on the river, but it is the verb meaning to rouse.
explanation.definitionFit: To arouse someone is to wake them from sleep, an older synonym.

clue.text: Dark time reportedly for Lancelot?

indicators.note: reportedly signals that the word is said aloud, giving a sound-alike spelt differently

parts.note: the dark time of day is night

explanation.surface: Asking whether a dark hour suits the Arthurian hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Lancelot is one of King Arthur's Round Table, an example of a knight, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Less than fifty percent? Very much so

definitions.meaning: taken literally, anything under fifty percent fails to reach one half
a British colloquial reply meaning emphatically yes

explanation.walkthrough: The British phrase is a strong affirmative, as in 'Did you enjoy it?' 'Not half!'; read literally it describes a share under one half.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally the phrase means a share under a half; as British slang it means absolutely yes.

clue.text: Group of people eating last of super meal

indicators.note: eating means the group takes that letter inside it

parts.note: a bunch is a group of people

indicators.note: last of asks for the final letter of super

explanation.surface: A crowd of diners finishing off a superb meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Brunch is a combined late-morning meal of breakfast and lunch.

clue.text: Soldier or sailor returning on leave

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece on another comes after it

parts.note: to leave a place or person is to desert them

indicators.note: returning means the word for sailor is read backwards

parts.note: a tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: A serviceman or sailor coming back home on leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desert Rats' was the nickname of the British 7th Armoured Division in North Africa in the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: A Desert Rat is a soldier of the British 7th Armoured Division, famed in the North African campaign.

clue.text: Black chicken decapitated

indicators.note: decapitated means the word loses its head, its first letter

parts.note: chicken as an adjective means cowardly, as does craven

explanation.surface: A grim farmyard scene of a dark-feathered hen beheaded.
explanation.definitionFit: Raven as an adjective describes glossy jet-black colour, like the bird's plumage.

clue.text: Mischievous child of eleven, German

definitions.meaning: an impish youngster, a little imp
the German word for the number eleven

explanation.surface: An eleven-year-old German boy causing trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: An imp or sprite is a mischief-maker, and a naughty little child is called one; it is also German for eleven.

clue.text: Fling before end of vacation brings complete happiness

indicators.note: before puts the throwing word ahead of that letter

parts.note: to fling is to throw, or heave

indicators.note: end of asks for the final letter of vacation

explanation.surface: A holiday romance at the end of a trip brings bliss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fling' looks like a holiday romance, but it is the verb meaning to throw.
explanation.definitionFit: Heaven is used figuratively for a state of perfect bliss or delight.

clue.text: Film star's account to head of RKO

indicators.note: head of asks for the first letter of RKO

explanation.surface: A movie star giving their story to the boss of the RKO studio.
explanation.walkthrough: RKO was a major Hollywood film studio.
explanation.definitionFit: A film star is a leading performer in films, a type of performer who plays roles.

clue.text: Drink from the bar, oddly

indicators.note: oddly asks for the first, third and fifth letters of the words the bar

explanation.surface: Ordering a drink from a pub counter, which is strange.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea is a hot drink brewed from leaves, an example of something one drinks.

clue.text: With every chance of success, I then messed up game of snooker

indicators.note: messed up means the letters of I then are put in disorder

parts.note: a single game in snooker is called a frame

explanation.surface: A snooker player admitting they then botched a game.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in contention, likely to win or be chosen, is the idiom's meaning; it can also mean under suspicion.
